newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Third World asks West for help for solar plans.
newsitem.headline: Third World asks West for help for solar plans.

text.p: A world solar conference dominated by Third World nations ended on Tuesday with calls on Western donors and rich countries to help fund ambitious plans to provide energy to those living without it.

Closing the World Solar Summit, Zimbabwean President Robert Mugabe said the conference's political pledges to help bring light to 2.4 billion people living without electricity around the globe would come to nought without financial backing.
"Without resources, this will remain a paper tiger," he said after two-days of deliberations, filled mostly by speeches.
"It is therefore important that this receives urgent attention...and a financial mechanism be established," he said.

A conference communique invited donors and private investors to start the process by helping to fund a 1996-2005 World Solar Programme prepared by the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation (UNESCO). Earlier, several delegates had also called on the West to help.

"We appeal to the international community, to the United Nations and its specialised agencies and the developed countries in particular, to provide the developing world with financial and technical assistance," Chinese state counsellor Luo Gan said.

International Energy Agency executive director Robert Priddle said the Third World's answer to financial problems lay in opening itself to foreign investment to develop the required solar and other renewable energy sources.
"Major private sector investment will be essential...those with the vision to liberalise energy markets and open up to outside investment would create exciting opportunities," he said.
Tanzanian President Benjamin Mkapa backed Priddle's statement, but said there was also great need to mobilise domestic savings through sound economic management.

The summit -- which was attended by delegates, including 12 heads of state and governments, from 100 countries -- was called to drum up political support for the use of solar and other renewable sources of energy.
But during the conference, a number of leaders shifted the focus to the need for financial assistance for a UNESCO programme to provide energy to all by the middle of the next century.
About 300 solar and other renewable sources of energy projects from 59 countries were presented to the summit, but no funding proposals were tabled despite the shift in emphasis.

On Monday, Pakistani President Farooq Ahmad Khan Leghari commended the World Bank for its recent pledge to help promote the use of solar and other renewable sources of energy, but said there was a disappointing lack of commitment from other donors.

"We hope that other multilateral agencies such as the Asian Development Bank, the Islamic Development Bank and also enlightened donor countries will commit themselves to the idea of the solar energy system and all such organisations will truly reflect this commitment through their programmes," he said.

Mugabe said funding for renewable energies averaged only three percent of multilateral banks' lending portfolios. He said this was ironic in view of the value of the emerging worldwide market for renewable energy technologies estimated at $40 billion a year.
